raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the first clinically established angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) for heart failure. Its development built on the recognition that neurohormonal blockade improves outcomes in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF): angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists each reduced mortality in pivotal trials [1-5]. Earlier “vasopeptidase” inhibition with omapatrilat supported the concept of simultaneous renin–angiotensin system and neprilysin blockade but was limited by angioedema, attributed partly to concurrent ACE and neprilysin inhibition [6]. Sacubitril/valsartan avoids ACE inhibition by combining a neprilysin prodrug with valsartan, thereby augmenting natriuretic peptides, bradykinin-independent vasodilation, natriuresis, and anti-fibrotic signalling while maintaining angiotensin II type-1 receptor blockade. Dose-ranging studies in hypertension demonstrated potent blood-pressure lowering and acceptable tolerability, encouraging heart-failure evaluation [7].

In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the phase 2 PARAMOUNT trial showed that LCZ696 reduced N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) more than valsartan at 12 weeks and suggested favourable left atrial remodelling [8]. However, the definitive mortality and morbidity breakthrough occurred in HFrEF. PARADIGM-HF randomised symptomatic ambulatory patients with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40%—later amended to ≤35%—to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril after sequential run-in periods [9]. The trial was stopped early because sacubitril/valsartan reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation, cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality, and heart-failure hospitalisation. Benefits were clinically meaningful and appeared early.

Subsequent analyses deepened understanding of these effects. Sacubitril/valsartan slowed clinical progression among survivors, reducing worsening symptoms, need for treatment intensification, emergency visits, and intensive-care use [10]. It reduced both sudden death and death from worsening heart failure compared with enalapril [11]. Treatment effects were consistent across age groups, including older patients, although hypotension and renal vulnerability require careful monitoring in frail patients [12]. Benefit was also preserved across the HFrEF ejection-fraction range studied [13]. Baseline systolic blood pressure modified tolerability more than efficacy: patients with lower pressure had higher absolute event rates, but the relative benefit remained evident, with symptomatic hypotension more common than with enalapril [14]. Additional analyses suggested modest improvement in glycaemic control among patients with diabetes [15], less severe hyperkalaemia when mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists were used [16], and slower decline in renal function compared with enalapril [17]. Patient-reported outcomes also favoured sacubitril/valsartan, with smaller deterioration in health-related quality of life [18].

Implementation requires attention to initiation and titration. Because neprilysin inhibition may increase angioedema risk when combined with ACE inhibitors, sacubitril/valsartan must not overlap with ACE inhibition and requires a washout period. TITRATION showed that gradual uptitration improves achievement of target dose in patients previously receiving low-dose renin–angiotensin system blockade [19]. PIONEER-HF extended use to patients hospitalised with acute decompensated HFrEF after haemodynamic stabilisation; compared with enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan produced a greater NT-proBNP reduction without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalaemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [20]. TRANSITION supported either in-hospital or early post-discharge initiation after stabilisation, reinforcing the hospitalisation as an opportunity to start disease-modifying therapy [21].

Reverse-remodelling data provide biological plausibility for outcome benefits. In PROVE-HF, NT-proBNP reduction after initiation correlated with improvements in LVEF, ventricular volumes, and atrial volume over 12 months [22]. EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant improvement in aortic characteristic impedance versus enalapril, but did show favourable changes in cardiac structure and biomarkers [23]. In patients with HFrEF and secondary functional mitral regurgitation, the PRIME trial found greater reduction in regurgitant volume with sacubitril/valsartan than valsartan, suggesting afterload, remodelling, and ventricular–valvular interactions may be therapeutically modifiable [24].

Evidence in HFpEF and mildly reduced EF is more nuanced. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalisations and cardiovascular death, but suggested heterogeneity, with greater apparent benefit in patients with LVEF below the median and in women [25,26]. A pooled analysis across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF indicated that benefit is greatest below normal EF and attenuates as EF rises, supporting current use particularly in HFrEF and selected patients with mildly reduced EF [27]. In acute myocardial infarction complicated by reduced EF, pulmonary congestion, or both, PARADISE-MI did not significantly reduce the primary composite compared with ramipril, so routine post-infarction substitution is not established [28].

In contemporary care, sacubitril/valsartan is a foundational HFrEF therapy alongside beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, whose benefit was established in trials such as DAPA-HF [29]. Guidelines recommend replacing ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker therapy with ARNI in eligible symptomatic HFrEF patients and support early initiation when feasible [30]. Remaining challenges include hypotension, affordability, renal monitoring, real-world uptitration, and defining benefit in very advanced disease and higher EF phenotypes. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan represents a major advance: it improves survival, reduces hospitalisation, favourably affects remodelling and symptoms, and has reshaped the therapeutic architecture of HFrEF.
